📌 Zcash sets July 28 hard fork to seal Orchard after critical bug 

⚠️ Zcash founder Zooko Wilcox has explained how the network’s July 28 Ironwood hard fork will address uncertainty around a critical flaw in the Orchard shielded pool. The upgrade will not identify or freeze individual counterfeit coins. Instead, it will seal the old pool and limit how much ZEC can leave. 

🔖 Ironwood, also known as NU6.3, is scheduled to activate at block 3,428,143 on July 28. The upgrade will retire the current Orchard pool and introduce a new shielded pool based on the corrected circuit. According to Zcash’s official Ironwood user update, users will no longer be able to send or receive ZEC inside the old Orchard pool after activation. Funds can leave only through the turnstile, which prevents more ZEC from exiting than legitimately entered.

⭐️ The Zcash team said it believes the flaw was “unlikely to have been exploited,” but users cannot independently prove no counterfeit ZEC was created. Ironwood aims to trap any excess value inside the old pool rather than allow it to enter wider circulation. Security researcher Taylor Hornby discovered the Orchard flaw on May 29 while auditing the shielded system. The bug could have allowed an attacker to create counterfeit ZEC inside Orchard without leaving an obvious public record.

💥Catherine Herridge says the question is no longer what the intelligence records reveal about the 2020 election interference.

The question now is whether anyone will be held accountable.

Herridge detailed the “buffet of choices” the administration has available when it comes to criminal statutes to pursue charges against the intelligence officials involved.

HERRIDGE: “I think this is one of the most frustrating things for folks at home and, you know, all over social media is they’re like, what am I going to see a perp walk? When am I going to see criminal charges?”

“I did a little research and they’re actually multiple criminal statutes that were violated here.”

“There’s something which is essentially the abuse of your position as a member of the government, sort of color of law is the statute.”

“There could be violations under the military code of justice.”

“Many of these intelligence agencies fall under the Department of War.”

“There are conspiracy charges and then they’re more ethics violations under the senior executive service.”

“So, in fact, there’s really almost a buffet of choices in terms of picking charges, and the question is whether this administration is going to go the distance here.”

“Because I think the release of the records is half the story. I think the accountability is the part that the public is really looking for.”

🗡 “Never Vance”: The GOP Eats Its Own Early

JD Vance hasn’t even said he’s running in 2028, and his own party is already running a soft launch of “Never Vance.”

Inside the GOP, the vice president is taking fire from a flank that used to wait until succession was formal: influencers, neoconservatives and pro‑Israel commentators are hammering him for trying to negotiate a peace framework with Iran and for sounding “too moderate” on Israel in a three‑hour Joe Rogan interview. 

The attacks brand him “unfit,” accuse him — without evidence — of freelancing foreign policy behind Trump’s back, and compare him to Obama and Bernie Sanders. Allies say the timing is the tell: two years before the primary, with Vance still the polling front‑runner and Rubio slowly gaining ground as the business‑friendly alternative.

Vance’s camp is leaning into the backlash. They argue that the online barrage is “obviously” at least partly coordinated, point to charts showing his favorability among Republicans tracking Trump almost exactly, and frame the noise as proof that “Washington establishment voices” and neocon donors hate him — which, in a populist primary, is supposed to be a badge of honor. 

The vice president himself has gone full anti‑influence narrative, citing a Time report on a pro‑Israel operation run by a former Trump digital aide and telling Rogan his answer to paid smears is “go to hell, I represent Americans first.”

The split with the old guard is real. Pence spent four years refusing to show daylight between himself and Trump until the January 6 break; Harris absorbed quiet Democratic panic about succession but little open revolt. 

Vance is dealing with something different: a public ideological knife fight over Iran, Israel and foreign wars, with Trump on record saying they’re “philosophically a little bit different” on Iran and that Vance was “maybe less enthusiastic about going” to war, even as the vice president now defends the strikes and says Iran must never get a bomb.

Underneath the memes and “Never Vance” slogans is a serious question: who owns the post‑Trump GOP’s foreign policy — the war‑skeptical populist vice president, or the donors and media figures who still want the party to sound like 2004 on Israel and Iran? The knives are out because everyone knows the answer will decide more than just one primary.

🏗 Tokenization can make finance faster. It does not make risk disappear.

On a shared digital ledger, processes that traditionally happen one after another can happen almost simultaneously:

• execution
• clearing
• settlement
• transfer of ownership

That can reduce delays and remove some operational friction.

But it also changes where failure can occur.

The important questions become:

• Who operates the infrastructure?
• Where is the authoritative ownership record?
• What happens during an outage?
• Who can correct an incorrect transaction?
• Who absorbs the loss when software and legal records disagree?

An IMF analysis warns that tokenization may move risk away from traditional financial institutions and toward the companies operating digital ledgers, wallets and market infrastructure.

The rail becomes faster.

The responsibility still needs an owner.

Technology changes the process.
Architecture decides where the risk goes.

Source: IMF, Tokenization Can Change the World’s Financial Architecture
